title: I spent 3 weeks refactoring our semantic chunking pipeline in production
body:
I built our team's first semantic chunking system three weeks ago, convinced it would solve our retrieval hallucination problem.

Instead, latency jumped 4x and our vector database bill doubled overnight.

Here is the raw architectural post-mortem and the 3 decisions that finally dropped retrieval errors by 68%:

1. Fixed vs Semantic Chunking:
We thought semantic chunking based on sentence embeddings was the holy grail. But chunk boundary drift caused related functions to get sliced in half. We reverted to recursive character chunking (800 token target, 150 token overlap) with document hierarchy metadata prepended to each chunk.

2. The Embedding Bottleneck:
Calling OpenAI text-embedding-3-small on 500k chunks dynamically on ingest was burning 42 minutes per index run. Moving to local bge-small-en-v1.5 running on ONNX runtime sliced indexing time to 4.2 minutes.

3. Reranking is 80% of the game:
Vector similarity alone retrieved superficially similar docstrings. Adding Cohere rerank-v3 as a secondary pass across top 25 candidates gave us the true quality jump.

```python
async def retrieve_chunks(query: str, top_k: int = 5):
    candidates = await vector_index.query(query, top_k=25)
    return reranker.rank(query, candidates)[:top_k]
```

title: Why our engineering team deleted 8,000 lines of LangChain boilerplate
body:
Six months ago, our codebase was suffocating under 4 different agent abstraction layers, custom memory wrappers, and endless prompt serialization bugs.

Last Friday, we merged a PR that deleted 8,240 lines and replaced them with 480 lines of typed native Python.

Here is what we learned migrating from heavyweight frameworks to native async primitives:

1. Explicit state machines beat hidden agent loops:
When an agent loops behind an abstract abstraction, debugging a failed tool call requires reading 8 stack frames of internal framework code. Using a typed Pydantic dataclass and an explicit while loop reduced our Mean-Time-To-Resolution from 2 hours to 8 minutes.

2. Native structured outputs:
With modern model APIs offering native JSON Schema validation, you no longer need output parsers with 500-line regex fallback handlers.

```python
response = await client.chat.completions.create(
    model='gpt-4o',
    messages=history,
    response_format={'type': 'json_object'}
)
```

3. Observability is trivial when state is flat:
We log each transition directly to SQLite with timestamp and latency. No black-box telemetry dashboards needed.

title: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)? A Beginner Guide
body:
Have you wondered how LLMs access private organizational data? The answer is RAG.

RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. It combines information retrieval with text generation.

The process works in three basic steps:
1. Ingestion: Documents are converted into vector embeddings.
2. Retrieval: Relevant passages are fetched based on semantic similarity.
3. Generation: The LLM answers the prompt using retrieved passages as context.

RAG helps reduce hallucinations and ensures up-to-date knowledge across modern organizations.

title: Introduction to Vector Databases and Cosine Similarity
body:
Vector databases have gained immense popularity recently. But how do they work?

Embeddings represent textual or multimodal data as arrays of floating-point numbers in high-dimensional space.

Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors to determine their semantic relationship.

Popular vector databases include Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, and pgvector. They are essential for modern AI applications.

title: We benchmarked Celery vs AsyncIO TaskGroups across 1,000,000 AI jobs
body:
We spent 2 weeks benchmarking Celery + Redis against native Python AsyncIO TaskGroups across 1M concurrent LLM inference routing tasks.

Here are the raw benchmark results and the architecture tradeoffs:

- Celery + Redis Worker Setup:
Throughput: 1,420 req/sec
p99 Latency: 420ms (Redis broker queue serialization overhead)
Memory Footprint: 2.4 GB across 16 worker processes

- Native Python 3.11 AsyncIO TaskGroups:
Throughput: 4,890 req/sec (+244% increase)
p99 Latency: 48ms (-88% reduction)
Memory Footprint: 380 MB

```python
async def process_batch(items: list[Job]):
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(run_job(job)) for job in items]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks]
```

The takeaway: For IO-bound LLM gateway routing, separate worker process overhead costs more than it saves. Keep IO in-process with bounded asyncio semaphores.

title: The $400 caching bug that crashed our vector search cluster
body:
At 2:15 AM last Tuesday, our vector database bill spiked by $400 in 3 hours because of a 4-line caching error.

Here is the bug post-mortem:

We implemented what we thought was an intelligent semantic cache. If a user query had cosine similarity > 0.94 with a prior query, we served cached embeddings.

Here was the mistake in our cache key hashing:
```python
# The Bug:
cache_key = f"{user_id}_{hash(query.strip().lower())}"
```

In Python, hash() is salted per process restart. Every time our ECS autoscaler spawned a container, the hash seed randomized. Queries missed cache 100% of the time, triggering a thundering herd of re-embeddings that overwhelmed our API quota.

The Fix:
Use deterministic SHA-256 with query canonicalization:
```python
cache_key = hashlib.sha256(canonicalize(query).encode()).hexdigest()
```

Always verify that your cache keys survive multi-process restarts. What was your team's most expensive production gotcha?

title: Why we stopped using LangGraph and built our own 120-line state graph
body:
Our multi-agent system required human-in-the-loop approvals, step checkpoints, and state rollbacks.

After fighting library version mismatches and complex checkpoint serializer bugs, we built an explicit typed state machine in 120 lines of pure Python.

Key architectural decisions:
1. State is an immutable Pydantic model.
2. Nodes are pure async functions `f(state) -> state`.
3. Transitions are validated by an explicit transition table.

```python
class Workflow:
    def __init__(self, transitions: dict):
        self.transitions = transitions
    
    async def step(self, state: State, action: str) -> State:
        next_node = self.transitions[state.current_stage][action]
        return await next_node(state)
```

Zero dependencies. 100% testable with pytest. Full visibility in 10 minutes.

title: How to Use SQLite in Python with SQLAlchemy
body:

To get started, install SQLAlchemy:
pip install sqlalchemy

Create your engine:
